newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer - "3.0" issue clouds German EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer - "3.0" issue clouds German EMU debate.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Wednesday that debate in Germany over the introduction of the euro was being obscured by a dispute over precise adherence to the Maastricht deficit criterion.

Adressing Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber during a Bundesbank reception, Tietmeyer said both houses of parliament had insisted as early as December 1992 that sustainable adherence to the entry criteria was crucial to the project of a European single currency.

Departing from the text of his speech, Tietmeyer said Stoiber was right to insist that conditions for transition to the single currency had to be right, but added: "I have the impression that the zero discussion has completely obscured the substance of the issue."

German politicians are currently arguing about whether the Maastricht requirement that budget deficits be limited to three percent of gross domestic product should be interpreted as 3.0 precisely, as demanded by Stoiber.
Stoiber has led a campaign for strict adherence to the Maastricht convergence criteria and wants the euro delayed if the deficit exceeds 3.0 percent of GDP.
Pressure from Stoiber forced Chancellor Helmut Kohl himself to say last week that three meant 3.0 -- despite the extra strain this will impose on Germany's fraught bid to qualify for monetary union.

Tietmeyer read out sentences from a text agreed by both houses of the German federal parliament in 1992 which stressed that the choice of EMU members had to be based on proven stability, convergence on economic fundamentals and sustainable budgetary and fiscal solidity.

"This is not a decision of the Bundesbank or a decision of the Bavarian state government. This is a decision of both houses of the federal parliament. It is an important orientation for the future for us all," he said.
